title: Hero Ball
part: PART THREE: THE HIGH AND THE HOLE

pages.text:
*Way to Lose #31: Score three goals and lose count of your team.*

The coin spins, landing on heads. I call it before it hits the grass, and I am right, because I have been winning lately. My legs feel like brand-new cleats, and my voice feels like a broadcast microphone. I look at Coach Gin. She is leaning against the yellow school bus, drinking tea. The vehicle is old, smelling strongly of diesel and stubborn determination.

"Coach," I say, pointing to myself and then to the field. "I have a plan. It is simple. Me. Ball. Net."

Gin lifts one eyebrow. A sunglass lens tilts up to reveal her eye. She does not blink, nor does she smile. She takes a long sip of her tea. The liquid sloshes in the steel thermos, sounding like rain hitting a tin roof.

"Losing is information," she says. Her voice is flat, the tone of a woman who has driven the same route for thirty years and knows exactly where every pothole lies.

I do not hear her. I am already looking at the opponent. They are the Bayside Barracudas. They are sunny, green, and look surprisingly soft. I step onto the field. The grass is wet. It squelches under my cleats. I am ready. I am the plan.
pages.image: A wiry girl with a high ponytail and yellow armband points at herself on a muddy field while a short woman in a yellow windbreaker and sunglasses sips from a steel thermos nearby.

pages.text:
The whistle screams, and the game is on. I win the ball at midfield, my stomach doing a backflip. There is a gap. I take it.

First defender: a boy in green. He slides in, but I step cleanly over his foot, the same effortless way I step over puddles on the way to school. Second: a red-haired girl. She rushes at me. I feint left, she goes left, and I cut right, leaving her tripping over her own shadow. Third: a big boy who tries to block my path. I dribble around his knee without looking up because I do not need to. Fourth: the last one. I leave him standing there, looking confused, like he just realized he forgot his wallet.

Now I am alone. The net is right in front of me. The crowd goes silent, then loud. I strike the ball. It flies into the top corner. This is the best shot of my life.

The cheer hits me. It is warm. It is sweet. It tastes exactly like the orange slices Ollie brings to the bench. I turn to scan the field. Ahmed is in the middle of the pitch. His hand is up. He is open. He is waiting for a pass. I do not look at him. I run to the corner flag. The noise is too good to stop.
pages.image: A girl sprints toward a soccer goal after dribbling past a sliding defender on a muddy field, her ponytail flying, while another player stands open in the background with a raised hand.

pages.text:
Half-time. The bench is a long plastic chair, cold enough to make my butt go numb, and I sit in the middle like I own the whole league.

Coach Gin walks over. She holds her thermos and does not yell, or smile, or even blink. She just looks at me with her one visible eye, steady as the bus mirror she probably used to drive with.

"How many passes did you make?" she asks.

I shrug because I don't count those. I count goals, and I count cheers, and I count the exact second the banner was unfurled.

Gin nods, then looks to her left. Ahmed is sitting there, staring at his shoes like they have personally insulted him. He does not say a word, but his silence is loud. It is a gong.

Priya sits next to Ahmed. She has her head in her gloves, her glasses fogged up, trying to disappear, trying to be small enough to fit inside her own elbows. I look at her, but I do not see her. I see the goal, and the banner, and the crowd.

Gin takes a sip of tea. "The scoreboard tells you what happened," she says.

She turns and walks away. Her windbreaker flaps. It makes a sound like a flag. I do not understand why my stomach feels tight.
pages.image: A short coach in a yellow jacket stands over a seated girl with a yellow armband, while a boy looks at his shoes and a girl with glasses hides her face in large gloves on a plastic bench.

pages.text:
Second half. The score is tied, 1 to 1, and I need more than just points. I need the world to know my name.

I get the ball again. I dribble past one defender, then hesitate. I don't pass; I keep it, driving forward because they are tired and slow while I am fast.

Goal two. The net ripples and the crowd roars.

Goal three. I shoot from the side, the ball bending into the corner. It is a hat-trick. I am on fire, gold, the sun.

Then, I have the ball in our own half. I am arrogant. I try a fancy move and lose the ball.

Two Sprouts attackers are coming. They are fast and angry, running straight at Priya.

She is alone, tiny, and shaking. The first shot comes; she dives and saves it, landing on the ground with wide eyes. The second shot is high and hard.

She jumps. Her gloves touch the ball, sending it into the crossbar. It bounces down and into the net.

I watch it happen. I do not move. I do not help. I am standing still, frozen in place. The score is 4 to 3. We are winning, but Priya is crying.
pages.image: A tiny goalkeeper with oversized gloves falls backward as a ball hits the crossbar, while a larger girl in a yellow armband stands still in the foreground, watching, with two opponents running toward the goal.

pages.text:
The whistle blows. Full time. We won, 4 to 3.

The crowd stands up, a wall of noise that chants, "DA-NI. DA-NI. DA-NI." It hits me like a gust of wind in a locker room, pushing me forward until Tank, who is huge and smiling, lifts me onto his shoulders.

I am up there. I can see the whole field, the ducks, the parking lot, and the bus.

Coach Gin is by the bus. She isn't clapping or cheering. She slides into the driver's seat and starts the engine, the low hum vibrating through the asphalt, a quiet sound that feels out of place in all the noise.

I look down at my team. They are hugging, shouting, and celebrating, but the chant is too loud, filling my ears and drowning out their voices.

I spot Priya on the ground. She hasn't stood up. She is looking at her gloves, her head bowed.

Ahmed is walking toward the bench, his eyes fixed on the dirt, not on me.

The chant continues. DA-NI. DA-NI. I smile and wave, feeling like the only person who matters, the star of the show, the hero of the day.

I don't hear a single teammate's voice. I don't know when they stopped talking or when they stopped looking at me. I only know that I am high, the noise is deafening, and the bus is waiting.
pages.image: A girl stands on the shoulders of a large boy, waving to a crowd, while a short woman in a yellow jacket sits in the driver's seat of a big blank yellow minibus, engine running, in the background.
